newsitem.title: FINLAND: EMU HAS SCANT ECON IMPACT, DECISION POLITICAL - FINNS.
newsitem.headline: EMU HAS SCANT ECON IMPACT, DECISION POLITICAL - FINNS.

text.p: Following are views on Finnish membership of the third stage of European economic and monetary union (EMU) by some Finnish experts published in a report by the Pellervo Economic Research Institute (PTT) received on Wednesday:
* Managing director Jaakko Iloniemi of the Centre for Finnish Business and Policy Studies (EVA) said the Euorpean single currency process is more a political project than an economic one.
"Foremost there is Germany seeking to avoid a situation where other EU-countries would ally against a Germany that is seen as too strong," he said.
On the other hand, France wants more say in European monetary policy, which has been controlled by the Bundesbank due to the central role of the German mark.
EMU seems to become the "hard core" of the European Union, an inner circle were matters will be prepared, he said.
Iloniemi said the thought that Finland could protect its national interests better outside the core than inside was "utopian".

* Professor Risto Seppala at the Finnish Forest Research Institute (METLA) said the Finnish chemical forest industry -- controlled by three big forestry groups -- has already made adjustments to operating in a global environment by diversifying its production geograpically and by strenghtened capital structures.
Participating in the single currency will not significantly change the conditions for these companies, he said.
But for mechanical forest industry companies, the single currency will mean an expansion of the home market and better financing possibilities.
Competion will become fiercer, which could be a serious challenge to companies with a weak capital structure.
Seppala expected raw wood prices to fall with the expanding markets. He viewed EMU membership as positive for the forestry sector.
* Forestry economist Ritva Toivonen said particularly the mechanical forest industry would benefit from the possibilities brought by EMU in the form of falling financing costs.
But she warned that there could be considerable risks and adjustment needs as well.
Competion will tighten, and paritcularly small companies with weak self-suffiency will have a hard time, she said.

For the sawmill industry, Sweden's decision to remain outside the first group of EMU countries will constitute a risk for Finnish companies as Finland has decided to join the single currency, Toivonen said.
* Professor Hannu Tervo from the University of Jyvaskyla said regional developments were largely irrelated to Finnish EMU membership.
The distribution of income and public services have so far effectively evened out welfare differences between regions, he said.
But the tight budget discipline linked to EMU could weaken conditions for the distribution of income, he added.

* PTT managing director Vesa Vihriala said Finland's economic development was largely indifferent to EMU membership. Therefore, in the short-term, membership of monetary union would not have any significant impact on the Finnish economy.
There are still many uncertainties surrounding the nature of EMU and Sweden's decision to remain outside weakened the attractiveness of joining.

As Finnish monetary policy has no credibility problems and as EMU membership marks an end to independent monetary policy, Vihriala said that from a narrow economic point of view it would be wisest for Finland to stay outside the single currency.

But political factors, such as securing Finland's say in European Union matters, could speak for membership in the first wave, he said. Political factors will be crucial when making the decision whether to join, he added.
